svg.title: I2C multi-controller bus access policies: timeline S3
svg.text: Three controllers under Poisson load, short packets
S3: 3 Poisson sources, 25 % offered load each, m = 0.1 Tmax = 2 ms; seeded arrivals, FIFO queues, empty at t = 0
50 ms = 2.5 Tmax shown (t = 35.32 s to 35.37 s); verdicts and utilisation from the full 50 s run
Tmax = 20 ms, tbuf = 0.78 µs, r = 60 µs (measured), margin = 10 µs, tidle = 10 µs, W = 100 µs
Tmax: 1024 bytes × 9 bit / 800 kbit/s (set 1 Mbit/s) = 11.52 ms + 2.7 ms clock stretching = 14.22 ms, rounded up to 20 ms
Controller A → target 0x10 (lowest address, wins ties)
transmitting (colour = sending controller, label = target address)
packet queued, holding off (re-arm r or policy deferral)
Arbitration is decided by the target address: of the controllers that START together, the one sending to the lowest address wins.
every controller gets the bus · worst access delay from arrival 80.0 ms = 4.00 Tmax
Bus busy → wait for STOP; arbitration lost → retry at once; after its own STOP a controller needs its re-arm time r before it competes again.
overloaded: the queues of A, B and C grow without bound
After its own STOP a controller waits Tmax + margin before it competes again.
every controller gets the bus · worst access delay from arrival 46.6 ms = 2.33 Tmax
After its own STOP a controller waits until the bus has been idle for tidle; controllers that have not had their turn compete as soon as the bus is free.
every controller gets the bus · worst access delay from arrival 47.7 ms = 2.38 Tmax
Before every attempt a controller probes the bus; bus busy or arbitration lost → back off a random time in (0, W] and probe again; after its own STOP it waits
time [ms]; darker gridlines every Tmax = 20 ms
Each controller receives packets of length m = 0.1 Tmax = 2 ms as an independent Poisson stream with 25 % offered load (75 % in total) and sends them in FIFO order.
Ticks above a lane mark arrivals; access delay = START of the winning transfer − packet arrival.
At this scale 1 px = 50 µs: tbuf = 0.78 µs, tidle = 10 µs, r = 60 µs, margin = 10 µs and W = 100 µs are far too small to draw, so adjacent bars that seem to touch are
in fact separated by such gaps.
Policy 1: the bus is free often enough that every controller is served, but the higher the address, the longer the wait: worst access delay C 80.0 ms, mean A 2.03, B
Policy 2 lets a controller send at most one packet per m + Tmax + margin = 22.01 ms, i.e. 9.1 % of bus time < 25 % offered: the queues grow without bound (3985,
4031, 3961 packets waiting after 50 s) while the bus is idle 72.7 % of the time.
Policy 3: worst access delay 46.6 ms, mean A 2.85, B 3.04, C 3.95 ms; utilisation 75.2 % ≈ offered load (50 s run). The delay counts from arrival: after a burst,
C's worst packet had 8 of C's own packets waiting ahead of it. From the head of its own queue a controller waits at most (N − 1 + k)·m plus gaps, with k = number
of lower target addresses: if its next packet arrives while it defers, every other controller may send once before the idle window and the lower addresses once more
after it. Here: A 4.01 ms ≤ 2 m, B 6.01 ms ≤ 3 m, C 8.02 ms ≤ 4 m. The round of (N − 1)·m holds only for saturated controllers.
Policy 4: worst access delay 47.7 ms, mean A 3.50, B 3.25, C 3.74 ms: the address no longer decides who waits (policy 1: C 5.39 ms). The bus stays idle after every
STOP until the first probe, so the mean over all packets rises to 3.50 ms (policies 1 and 3: 3.27 and 3.28 ms). The wait from the head of the own queue has no bound,
only a probability: here A 15.8, B 18.1, C 24.3 ms (policy 3: ≤ (N − 1 + k)·m). Each controller probes about 3 500 times per second.
Window: policies 1 and 3 give every transfer to the same controller until t = 195 ms (they only shift STARTs by microseconds) and to different controllers in 14.1 %
of all transfers of the run. Shown is the stretch in which policy 1 delays C longest: as long as A and B both have packets queued they alternate and C waits, while
policy 3 serves A, B and C in turn. Both serve the whole offered load, so their utilisation is the same; they only change who sends when.
